**Answer**

The “privileges of the birth‑empire” referred to the Romanov rule in the **Russian Empire –** the sovereign, noble and imperial prerogatives that Alexey Brodovitch inherited at birth.  
These privileges were **abolished by the February Revolution (1917)**, which saw Tsar Nicholas II abdicate, the monarchy end, and a provisional government (together with the Petrograd Soviet) take charge of a fledgling Russian republic. The same 1917 Revolution also dismantled the legal and social privileges that had characterised the imperial order.

**And, as a related historical context,** the **Habsburg Monarchy (Austro‑Hungarian Empire)** likewise dissolved – but later, in 1918–19, after World I and the collapse of the empire, new independent states (e.g., the Republics of Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, etc.) emerged.  

So, the February Revolution in 1917 ended the Romanov privileges of the Russian Empire, while the Habsburg monarchy dissolved a few years later, at the end of World I.

**Thuringia** (English: [/θ ə ˈ r ɪ n dʒ i ə/]; [German]: _Thüringen_[[ˈtyːʁɪŋən]][][ⓘ] officially the **Free State of Thuringia**, _Freistaat Thüringen_[[ˈfʁaɪʃtaːt ˈtyːʁɪŋən]]) is a landlocked [state] in central [Germany]. With 2.1 million people, it is 12th-largest by population, and with 16,171 square kilometers, it is 11th-largest in area.[[5]] It is the country's centermost state.

[Erfurt] is the capital and largest city. Other cities include [Jena], [Gera] and [Weimar]. Thuringia is bordered by [Bavaria], [Hesse], [Lower Saxony], [Saxony], and [Saxony-Anhalt]. It has been known as "the green heart of Germany" (_das grüne Herz Deutschlands_) from the late 19th century due to its broad, dense forest.[[6]] Most of Thuringia is in the [Saale][drainage basin], a [left-bank tributary] "Bank (geography)") of the [Elbe].

The [Frankish][Duchy of Thuringia] was established around 631 AD by [King Dagobert I]. The modern state was established in 1920 by the [Weimar Republic] through a merger of the [Ernestine duchies], save for [Saxe-Coburg]. After [World War II], Thuringia came under the [Soviet occupation zone] in [Allied-occupied Germany], and its borders were reformed, to become [contiguous]. Thuringia became part of the [German Democratic Republic] in 1949, but was dissolved in 1952 during [administrative reforms], and divided into the Districts of [Erfurt], [Suhl] and [Gera]. Thuringia was re-established in 1990 following [German reunification], slightly re-drawn, and became one of the [new states] of the Federal Republic of Germany.

**Answer**

The “privileges of the birth‑empire” referred to the Romanov rule in the **Russian Empire –** the sovereign, noble and imperial prerogatives that Alexey Brodovitch inherited at birth.  
These privileges were **abolished by the February Revolution (1917)**, which saw Tsar Nicholas II abdicate, the monarchy end, and a provisional government (together with the Petrograd Soviet) take charge of a fledgling Russian republic. The same 1917 Revolution also dismantled the legal and social privileges that had characterised the imperial order.

**And, as a related historical context,** the **Habsburg Monarchy (Austro‑Hungarian Empire)** likewise dissolved – but later, in 1918–19, after World I and the collapse of the empire, new independent states (e.g., the Republics of Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, etc.) emerged.  

So, the February Revolution in 1917 ended the Romanov privileges of the Russian Empire, while the Habsburg monarchy dissolved a few years later, at the end of World I.
